list.listitem: Most episodes of pharyngitis are due to viruses; approximately 20% to 30% are due to group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus (GABHS). B
Most episodes of pharyngitis, including those due to GABHS, are self-limiting and do not require testing for the presence of GABHS nor a prescription of antibiotics.B

Appropriate triage should be undertaken when evaluating patients presenting with acute pharyngitis to distinguish those with apparently uncomplicated pharyngitis and low risk for acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) from those with potentially complicated pharyngitis or moderate to high risk for RHD.C

When undertaken, the evaluation for GABHS pharyngitis should include a focused history and physical examination, guided by validated clinical decision rules, and confirmed by rapid antigen detection testing (RADT), throat culture, or a molecular assay for group A streptococcus. C

Consider Lemierre's syndrome in critically ill patients with pharyngitis, as well as those with prolonged pharyngitis or pharyngitis that improves and then worsens (especially older children and adolescents). C
Penicillin is the treatment of choice for GABHS pharyngitis. B

background.definition: Pharyngitis is an inflammatory illness of the mucous membranes and underlying structures of the throat.

list.listitem: Acute pharyngitis is responsible for more than 6 million office visits each year by children younger than 15 years.
Acute pharyngitis accounts for 1.8 million visits by adolescents and young adults between the ages of 15 and 24 years.
Pharyngitis can be caused by many different pathogens.
Viruses are the most common cause of acute pharyngitis in children.
The most common viruses causing pharyngitis are adenovirus; influenza viruses A and B; parainfluenza viruses 1, 2, and 3; Epstein-Barr virus; and enteroviruses such as coxsackievirus.
GABHS is the most common bacterial cause of acute pharyngitis, accounting for 15% to 30% of cases of acute pharyngitis in children.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a cause of acute pharyngitis in sexually active teenagers.
Other bacterial causes include groups C and G beta-hemolytic streptococci, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, and Fusobacterium necrophorum.
Large respiratory droplets typically transmit the organism from person to person.
The organism invades the pharyngeal mucosa, causing local inflammation.
Person-to-person contact enhances the spread of infection.
The rate of GABHS transmission from an infectious case to close contacts is approximately 35%. The incubation period for GAS pharyngitis is 2 to 4 days.

Patients presenting with acute sore throat should undergo screening prior to testing for GABHS. Patients triaged to have apparently uncomplicated pharyngitis and at low risk for ARF/RHD should not undergo further workup.C

A Cochrane review found limited evidence from poor-quality trials that immunostimulants may prevent acute respiratory tract infections in children. Better quality studies are needed before this can be recommended.B

Use a method of triage that incorporates a validated clinical decision rule (such as the Centor or McIsaac score) for patients with acute sore throat to initially detect those with risk for suppurative complications or sepsis (, , and ) as well as those with risk for later sequelae such as rheumatic heart disease (Image 4) when determining whether to test for GABHS.B
A positive rapid antigen detection test (RADT) result or throat culture provides enough evidence to support the diagnosis of GABHS pharyngitis. C
A molecular assay may be used in place of RADT and throat culture, and does not require a follow up throat culture if negative.C

If an RADT is obtained and the results are negative, clinicians may wish to consider culture confirmation in children who have a very high risk for streptococcal pharyngitis. While traditionally guidelines have recommended a throat culture following a negative RADT, there is evidence to question that recommendation.C
Be suspicious of Fusobacterium necrophorum in a patient with severe signs and symptoms of bacterial pharyngitis or prolonged or recurrent symptoms and negative GABHS testing.C
Patients who present with signs and symptoms suggestive of a viral pharyngitis require no further evaluation.C
Be highly suspicious of gonococcal pharyngitis if a sexually active teenager presents with sore throat, arthralgias, dysuria, and rash. C

list.listitem: GABHS pharyngitis is seen more commonly during the winter and spring. Peritonsillar abscess is a rare complication; suspect it in children presenting with "hot potato" voice and sudden, severe onset of symptoms.

Elements of the history and physical examination that best rule in GABHS pharyngitis are tonsillar or pharyngeal exudates, fever, anterior cervical adenopathy, and absence of cough. Patients with coryza, cough, conjunctivitis, hoarseness, oropharyngeal lesions (ulcers, vesicles), diarrhea, and absence of fever are more likely to have a viral pharyngitis.
Palatine petechiae and scarlatiniform rash are uncommon findings, but are very specific for GABHS pharyngitis.

Patients who present with sore throat and prominent fatigue, fever, adenopathy (especially posterior), and hepatosplenomegaly should be tested for infectious mononucleosis (IM). The most helpful finding that increases the likelihood of IM is the presence of adenopathy in regions other than the anterior cervical chain.
Adolescents with unusually severe signs and symptoms of pharyngitis should be evaluated for rare throat infections (such as peritonsillar abscess, parapharyngeal abscess, epiglottitis).
Lemierre syndrome should be considered in patients presenting with severe pharyngitis, neck pain and respiratory distress or chest pain.
Patients whose clinical presentation suggests potentially complicated pharyngitis or moderate to high risk for RHD should undergo further evaluation.

Throat culture is the gold standard for the confirmation of acute GABHS pharyngitis. However, rapid antigen detection tests (RADTs) are most frequently used for diagnosis owing to ease of use, reliability, and rapidity of results. RADTs have an overall sensitivity of 80% to 95% and a specificity of 95% or greater.

Molecular tests, such as nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, may be used in place of a RADT, and, if negative, do not require a follow up throat culture due to the high sensitivities (>97%-100%) of the tests. However, due to their high sensitivity, they are more likely to be positive in asymptomatic individuals ('carriers').
Children with suspected viral pharyngitis (ie, cough, no fever, no adenopathy, and no exudates) should not undergo evaluation for GABHS pharyngitis.
GABHS pharyngitis testing should generally not be performed in children younger than 3 years of age, as GABHS rarely causes pharyngitis in this age and rheumatic fever is uncommon.

Anti-streptococcal antibody (ASO) titers are not recommended as they reflect past infection, not current infection. Diagnostic testing or empiric treatment of asymptomatic household contacts is also not recommended.

If infectious mononucleosis is suspected, especially in adolescents and young adults, consider ordering a CBC and heterophile antibody test. The heterophile antibody test has poor sensitivity in children younger than 13 years and early in the course of infection.More than 10% atypical lymphocytes and >40% lymphocytes are also strong evidence in favor of infectious mononucleosis as the cause. If infectious mononucleosis is suspected in children younger than 13 years, IgM antibody for the Epstein-Barr viral capsid antigen may be the preferred test due to lack of sensitivity of the monospot in this age group, particularly early in the course of the illness.
If gonococcal pharyngitis is suspected, NAAT is preferred over culture due to the higher sensitivity. If pharyngeal culture is performed, it should be processed on Thayer-Martin agar.
Fusobacterium necrophorum, which causes Lemierre's syndrome, is difficult to isolate by routine throat culture due to its anaerobic nature, and routine testing is not currently recommended.

For critically ill patients with pharyngitis, as well as those with prolonged pharyngitis or pharyngitis that improves and then worsens (especially older children and adolescents), consider Lemierre's syndrome. Diagnostic evaluation includes blood and throat cultures including culture specific for fusobacterium necrophorum, and imaging of the neck and chest.
The Centor Score was originally developed in adults in the emergency department in Alabama.

The McIsaac score was independently derived based on a cohort of patients presenting to a primary care clinic. In essence, it modifies the Centor score by including age as an extra variable, adding a point for ages 3 to 14, and subtracting a point for those aged ≥45 years.

Both models were validated in a study of 206,870 patients. In patients older than 15 years, 7% with a Centor Score of 0 and 12% with a score of 1 tested positive for GABHS pharyngitis. In patients 3 to 15 years, 8% with a McIsaac score of 0 and 14% with a score of 1 tested positive for GABHS.
Attia and colleagues developed and validated a risk score specific for children.

There is concern for furthering antibiotic resistance and causation of adverse events due to over treatment with antibiotics in high-income countries, where incidence of suppurative and non-suppurative complications are extremely rare.
Traditional recommended management is outlined in
See for calculation of the McIsaac risk score for strep and for suggested management.
Suspect infectious mononucleosis in children and adolescents with persistent symptoms, significant adenopathy (especially posterior), or prominent fatigue.
Use supportive care only (acetaminophen for fever or pain, sufficient fluids) for uncomplicated pharyngitis. A
Individuals triaged to have moderate to high risk of complicated pharyngitis or risk for ARF/RHD should be evaluated for identification and treatment of GABHS. See .C
Penicillin VK is the treatment of choice for GABHS pharyngitis; amoxicillin is an acceptable alternative. B
In countries where ARF is uncommon, but antibiotics are deemed necessary, a short course of antibiotics for 5 days has been shown to be non-inferior to a 10 day course.B
Corticosteroids play no role in the treatment of GABHS pharyngitis, though they may play a small role, in a single dose, to improve pain in strep-negative pharyngitis. B
Macrolides and cephalosporins are appropriate as alternative therapy in patients allergic to penicillin. B

Symptoms of severe pharyngitis (difficulty swallowing, drooling, neck tenderness, or swelling) and a negative GABHS test should prompt evaluation for and possibly empiric treatment of presumed Fusobacterium necrophorum in adolescents. C
If treating for suspected Fusobacterium necrophorum, avoid use of macrolides and cephalosporins in favor of penicillin or clindamycin. B
Use supportive care only (acetaminophen for fever or pain, sufficient fluids) for uncomplicated pharyngitis.

Acute pharyngitis, including that caused by GABHS, is a self-limited illness and does not routinely require antibiotic treatment in high-income countries (North America and Western Europe) where ARF and RHD are extremely rare, with exceptions for a few high-risk individuals such as immigrants from low-income countries, and persons of low-socio-economic populations. See .,,,

Antibiotics should be discouraged for patients without documented bacterial infection. Effective strategies include communication strategies and individualized antibiotic prescribing feedback reports.

A Cochrane review concluded that antibiotics probably reduce the number of people experiencing sore throat, reduce the likelihood of headache, and some sore throat complications. The benefits are more modest than commonly thought: reduction in symptoms by a mean of 16 hours, and a NNT of 6 for reduced sore throat at day 3 and 18 at one week. While the prevalence of suppurative complications was low, there was a lower risk of suppurative complications such as acute otitis media (Peto odds ratio 0.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.40, 10 studies with 3646 children) and peritonsillar abscess (Peto OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.35, 8 studies with 2433 children) but not acute sinusitis. They also lowered the risk of acute rheumatic fever (Peto OR 0.36, 95% CI0.26 to 0.50, 18 studies with 12,249 children), but it should be noted that the overall prevalence of acute rheumatic fever was very low, particularly in the later studies. There were too few children with acute glomerulonephritis to allow for meaningful conclusions. The majority of included studies were conducted in the 1950s, during which time the rates of serious complications (especially acute rheumatic fever) were much higher than today.

Streptococcus carriers are unlikely to spread the organism to close contacts, and are at little risk of suppurative and nonsuppurative complications. Among asymptomatic children, the prevalence of GABHS carriage is 12%. Treatment of and attempts to eradicate the carrier state remain controversial.

In adolescents and young adults presenting with symptoms of severe or persistent pharyngitis (difficulty swallowing, drooling, neck tenderness, or swelling) and a negative GABHS test, consider Fusobacterium necrophorum. Empiric therapy with penicillin or clindamycin can be considered in these patients.

A Cochrane review found no clinically meaningful differences between different antibiotics for GABHS pharyngitis. Therefore, considering the low cost, narrow spectrum and absence of resistance, penicillin is still recommended as the first antibiotic of choice.

Penicillin VK 250 mg given 2 or 3 times per day for 10 days is the treatment of choice for GABHS pharyngitis if the patient weighs less than 27 kg. If the patient weighs more than 27 kg, use 500 mg 2 or 3 times per day for 10 days. Intramuscular benzathine penicillin may be used for more rapid resolution or for patients unable to or unlikely to follow the recommended oral regimen.
Amoxicillin liquid is as efficacious as penicillin VK and is often used in children because of its better taste and therefore potentially better compliance.
Among patients with a history of rheumatic fever, intramuscular penicillin was more effective than oral penicillin, and injections every 2 weeks were more effective than every 4 weeks.

First-generation cephalosporins can be used for penicillin-allergic patients provided this allergy is not an immediate-type hypersensitivity to beta-lactams (i.e.,anaphylaxis). Other alternatives include clindamycin for 10 days, clarithromycin for 10 days, or azithromycin for 5 days. A meta-analysis of 35 studies showed that bacteriologic cure was significantly more likely with cephalosporin treatment when compared with penicillin; however, the effect of cephalosporin treatment on the prevention of rheumatic heart disease is unknown.
Avoid macrolides if choosing to treat streptococcus-negative pharyngitis empirically.

A large Swedish randomized trial of moderate to severe GABHS pharyngitis (3 or 4 Centor criteria) in 105 children and 317 adults compared penicillin 800 mg 4 times daily for 5 days with penicillin 1000 mg 3 times a day for 10 days. Patients receiving the shorter course also had a shorter duration of symptoms and no difference in relapse rates. They also had fewer adverse events.

Once-daily amoxicillin has been studied, but its use remains controversial as its impact on preventing acute rheumatic fever is unclear.Similarly, while a systematic review found similar symptomatic benefit to shorter duration therapy (2-6 days), especially for azithromycin, the impact of this approach on rheumatic fever prevention and bacterial resistance is of concern.

A randomized double-blind controlled trial of 150 children between the ages of 5 and 18 years with pain from acute pharyngitis showed that although corticosteroids (dexamethasone) were effective in pain resolution for 24 hours, only patients with negative strep tests were likely to benefit.

A systematic review found 7 studies of limited quality, 3 of which found limited benefit to the use of corticosteroids in infectious mononucleosis pharyngitis. A Cochrane review of the use of steroids as an adjuvant to antibiotics in sore throat found more people to have resolution of throat pain within 24 hours (RR 3.2; 95% CI 2.0-5.1). However, there were few children included in the trials.

Referral to an ear, nose, and throat specialist for tonsillectomy may be indicated for children who present with recurrent episodes (more than 6 in a 12-month period) of severe bacterial pharyngitis. A Cochrane systematic review found that children with recurrent acute tonsillitis will avoid 0.6 episodes of sore throat in the first year after adeno/tonsillectomy (3.0 vs 3.6 episodes).
Tonsillectomy has not been found to be helpful in children with less severe episodes of pharyngitis.
A systematic review did not find a consistent benefit to routine use of antibiotics following tonsillectomy, although the practice is common.

A systematic review found some evidence to support the use of Chinese medicinal herbs, but due to the lack of high quality clinical trials, the efficacy of Chinese medicinal herbs for treating pharyngitis is controversial.
Acute rheumatic fever is the most serious complication of GABHS pharyngitis.
Although pharyngitis is a self-limited disease, appropriate treatment of GABHS pharyngitis initiated within 9 days of the onset of pharyngitis has been shown to prevent acute rheumatic fever.
Other complications of GABHS pharyngitis include peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, Lemierre syndrome, cervical lymphadenitis, and acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Lemierre syndrome, characterized by bacteremia, internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis, and metastatic septic emboli secondary to acute pharyngeal infections, should be suspected in patients with persistent high fever and neck pain with tenderness, dyspnea, pleurisy, and/or hemoptysis.
Pharyngitis is a self-limited disease. C
Appropriate antimicrobial treatment of GABHS pharyngitis prevents rheumatic fever and other nonsuppurative and suppurative complications. C
Pharyngitis symptoms usually resolve within 5 to 10 days.

Patients with GABHS pharyngitis, if left untreated, may develop complications such as acute rheumatic fever (3% risk worldwide), peritonsillar abscesses, and retropharyngeal abscesses. It is not certain if treatment with antibiotics reduces the risk of developing poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Patients are infectious during the acute illness and for approximately 1 week after that.
Acute pharyngitis, including GABHS pharyngitis, is a self-limited disease.
In a community-based study that included children who did not seek care from a physician, most children with sore throat had largely resolved their symptoms in 7 to 10 days.
Appropriate antimicrobial treatment of patients with GABHS pharyngitis prevents acute rheumatic fever.
Antibiotic treatment reduces the duration of symptoms by approximately 12 to 24 hours on average.
There is no need to routinely perform follow-up throat cultures or RADTs for asymptomatic patients who have completed an appropriate course of antibiotics.
Perform a follow-up throat culture on patients with a history of rheumatic fever.
Patients should remain well hydrated and may use acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever control.
Patients should contact their physician if symptoms have not resolved within 7 to 10 days.
